title: 2 Kings 25:22–30
context: Nebuchadnezzar appoints Gedaliah son of Ahikam governor over those left in Judah; Gedaliah urges the captains to serve Babylon and live, but Ishmael of the royal line kills him at Mizpah, and the people flee to Egypt in fear of the Chaldeans. In the thirty-seventh year of his exile, Jehoiachin is released from prison by Evilmerodach, given a seat of honor, and provided for all his life. Both traditions read this as shared ground; the release is not a restoration of the kingdom, though both may note that the Davidic line is not extinguished (cf. 2 Sam 7:12–16; Jer 52:31–34).

verses.text: As for the people who were left in the land of Judah whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, even over them he made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, governor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Over those left in the land, “even over them he made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, governor.” Arminian readers note that Gedaliah’s family had served under Josiah (22:3) and that Ahikam had protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24).

The appointment offers stability for those left in the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a measure of order provided for the remnant.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Jeremiah 39:14 and 40:5–6 show Jeremiah living with Gedaliah, and the governor’s role is presented as a hopeful arrangement.

verses.text: Now when all the captains of the forces, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.
verses.arminianNotes:
The captains of the forces come to Gedaliah at Mizpah, including Ishmael son of Nethaniah and Johanan son of Kareah. Arminian readers note that the remaining leaders gather around the new governor.

Jeremiah 40:7–8 gives a parallel account.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see an attempt to rebuild life in the land.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the list of names prepares for the tragedy that follows.

verses.text: Gedaliah swore to them and to their men, and said to them, “Don’t be afraid because of the servants of the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Gedaliah says, “Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.” Arminian readers note that his counsel matches Jeremiah’s message (cf. Jer 27:12).

He offers a path of peace under Babylon’s rule.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Gedaliah’s counsel echoing the prophet’s word.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: accepting the judgment and seeking peace was the course the LORD’s prophet had urged.

verses.text: But in the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the royal offspring came, and ten men with him, and struck Gedaliah so that he died, with the Jews and the Chaldeans that were with him at Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the royal offspring came, and ten men with him, and struck Gedaliah so that he died.” Arminian readers note the tragedy of the murder.

Jeremiah 40:14 says Gedaliah had been warned; Jeremiah 41:1–3 gives more detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see violence from within Judah ending the hope of stability.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read it soberly: the narrative reports the murder without speculating beyond the text.

verses.text: All the people, both small and great, and the captains of the forces arose and came to Egypt; for they were afraid of the Chaldeans.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the people, both small and great, and the captains of the forces arose and came to Egypt; for they were afraid of the Chaldeans.” Arminian readers note the people’s fear.

Jeremiah 42–43 records that Jeremiah urged them not to go to Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the remnant leaving the land in fear.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the flight to Egypt is reported as narrative, with fuller detail in Jeremiah 41–43.

verses.text: In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, Evilmerodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, released Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison,
verses.arminianNotes:
In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, “Evilmerodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, released Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison.” Arminian readers note the change in his circumstances.

Jeremiah 52:31 gives the twenty-fifth day rather than the twenty-seventh; the difference is noted without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the release and the date difference with Jeremiah 52:31.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the release is a real kindness, but it is not a restoration of the kingdom.

verses.text: and he spoke kindly to him and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon,
verses.arminianNotes:
Evilmerodach “spoke kindly to him and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon.” Arminian readers note the honor given to Jehoiachin among the exiled kings.

The honor is real, though he remains in Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a measure of favor shown to the Davidic king in exile (cf. 1 Kings 8:50).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the book records the kindness without claiming that the kingdom is restored.

verses.text: and changed his prison garments. Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king “changed his prison garments.” “Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life.” Arminian readers note the change in Jehoiachin’s daily life.

He lives under the Babylonian king’s provision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a modest sign that the house of David is preserved.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both note as a hedged option that the line of David is not extinguished (cf. 2 Sam 7:14–16), though the book does not develop the point.

verses.text: and for his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him from the king, every day a portion, all the days of his life.
verses.arminianNotes:
The book says that “for his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him from the king, every day a portion, all the days of his life.” Arminian readers note the steady provision for Jehoiachin.

The book ends with the king still in exile.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the ending as restrained: no return, no restored throne, yet the Davidic king survives (cf. Jer 52:31–34).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the closing verses leave readers with a quiet note of continuity, not a full restoration.
